w:r.w:t: Mesenchyme (embryonic connective tissue) differentiates into hyaline cartilage.
The hyaline cartilage forms a "bony" shape.
The perichondrium around the cartilage is vascularized, causing differentiation of mesenchymal cells into osteoblasts.
Those osteoblasts start forming a bone collar around the chondrocytes and creating primary ossification center.
The bone collar blocks nutrients to the chondrocytes in the center of the diaphysis, causing them to hypertrophy and die.
A periosteal bud (blood vessels canal) breaks through the bone collar (with the help of osteoclast) supplying nutrients to the diaphysis.
The periosteal bud causes the formation of osteoblasts in the diaphysis which will start building bone matrix from the primary ossification center.
Elongation of the outer compact bone and inner spongy bone is done by the osteoblasts.
Osteoclasts migrate into the diaphysis through the circulation, starting to create medullary cavities which will house the bone marrow.
During childhood the primary and secondary ossification centers are separated by the
that helps in bone elongation, in adulthood that the disk disappears, stopping bone growth.
Metaphysis- cartilaginous growth plate (ossifies at adulthood).
Epiphysis- hyaline cartilage which will go through secondary ossification after birth.
Bone remodeling is a process that is continuous throughout life. This process is composed of two parts: bone resorption and ossification.

Bone resorption occurs constantly by osteoclasts that break down bone, while ossification occurs constantly by osteoblasts the form bone tissue. This mechanism is the remodeling, and it usually responds to functional demands of the mechanical load on the body.
Dysfunction of the remodeling process can cause bone metabolic diseases like, osteoporosis (weakness of bones).
After endochondral ossification of long bones, the epiphysis and the metaphysis are still composed of hyaline cartilage (not ossified).
During infancy, secondary ossification occurs, and the epiphysis transforms from cartilage into bone.
The metaphysis remains cartilaginous (hyaline). This cartilage will go through a process that will cause bone elongation. This process occurs from infancy to about 20 years old.

The epiphyseal growth plate located inside the metaphysis can be divided into 4 regions (epiphyseal end → diaphyseal end): reserve zone, proliferative zone, zone of maturation and zone of calcified matrix.
contains small chondrocytes and matrix. This area does not participate in bone growth, it secures the epiphyseal plate to the epiphysis.
contains larger chondrocytes than the reserve zone. In this area mitotic division of chondrocytes occurs, these chondrocytes replace the ossified chondrocytes.
is the area in which the newly formed chondrocytes from the proliferative zone mature, increasing in size.

is the area in which the matrix is calcified, and the chondrocytes die. Osteoblasts and blood vessels from the diaphysis penetrates this area, forming it into bone tissue. This area connects the epiphyseal plate into the metaphysis.

**Trauma to the bone- when trauma as fracture happens to the bone. The broken ends need to be brought together as close as possible to normal position. When the bone heals, the fibroblasts in the surrounding periosteum, proliferate and secrete collagen. This forms the collar of callus to hold the bones together. Bone remodeling occurs in the fracture area and the callus calcifies, and eventually reabsorbs to be replaced by bone. After several months little evidence to the fracture is evident.

Sinusitis = inflammation of sinuses (on an x-ray, black sinus = healthy, full of air // white sinus – inflammation, full of pathological fluid).
Sinusitis can be caused by: common cold, allergy, and rhinitis (=inflammation of the mucous membrane inside the nose).

These are the most superior in location. They drain into the nasal cavity via the frontonasal duct, which opens to the middle nasal meatus.

Numerous variable cavities separated by thin, in-complete walls within the ethmoid- forming the ethmoidal labyrinth. Each side of the ethmoidal cells is divided into anterior, middle, and posterior groups.

The largest cell, the ethmoidal bulla is located on the lateral nasal wall above the hiatus semilunaris. Its medial border is with the upper part of the nasal cavity and laterally with the orbit from which they are separated by only a paper-thin plate of bone.

They are adjacent from above to the anterior cranial fossa and from below to the maxillary sinus. Anterior and middle open to the middle nasal meatus and the posterior open into the superior nasal meatus.
The largest of the paranasal sinuses, completely filling the body of the maxilla.
Its roof is the floor of the orbit.
Anteriorly and latterly the maxillary sinus is bounded to the facial surface of the maxilla, posteriorly it is the maxillary tuberosity and medially it borders with the nasal cavity.
The maxillary sinus opens through the roof into the middle nasal meatus.
Lies in the body of the sphenoid behind the nasal cavity. A septum divides the variable right and left sphenoidal sinuses and it may deviate to one side.

The anterior border is with the ethmoidal cells, anteriorly and superiorly with the optic canal, posteriorly and superiorly with the hypophyseal fossa (the house of the pituitary gland) and laterally with the carotid sulcus.
The relationships of this sinus are of clinical importance – the pituitary gland can be surgically accessed via passing through the nasal roof, into the sphenoid sinus and through the sphenoid bone.

Internal structure of lungs - alveoli and their microscopic structure, surfactant, development, and maturation of lungs

Alveoli are the terminal air spaces of the respiratory system and are the actual sites of gas exchange between the air and the blood. The surface area available for gas exchange is increased by the lung alveoli. Each alveolus is surrounded by a network of capillaries that brings blood into close proximity to inhaled air inside the alveolus.
About 150 to 250 million alveoli are found in each adult lung, their combined internal surface area is approximately 75 m2, the size of a tennis court.
Each alveolus is a thin-walled polyhedral chamber approximately 0.2 mm in diameter that is combined with an alveolar sac.
